items.title: 8 tankers hit over the weekend, 3 on fire — and oil still sold off
items.idea: HFIR: 8 tankers attacked in the Oman Lane, at least 3 burning, flow trackers show a visible slowdown. Oil fell anyway because post-midterm 'renewed strikes' positioning got rinsed by peace-deal headlines. Physical market shows no panic: Saudis have unsold cargoes and Aramco cut OSP again.
items.angle: Paper and physical are pointing in opposite directions. Positioning data lands Friday — a flush plus escalation tail is an asymmetric setup for energy.
items.tweetA: Eight tankers attacked, three on fire, and Brent down. That's not a market pricing risk, that's a market that got long the wrong headline and got flushed. The tail didn't go away — the positioning did. $XLE $OXY
items.tweetB: Aramco cutting OSP again while tankers burn tells you who's the forced seller. Saudis are pushing barrels ahead of escalation, or they know something about demand. Either way the physical bid isn't there. $USO $CVX

charts.desc: Charts inside — worth opening (storage, flow trackers)

items.title: Saudi output 10.5 mb/d, but only ~9 mb/d actually supplied
items.idea: Energy Aspects (via HFIR): Saudi lifted October production to 10.5 mb/d, effectively ending any shut-in, yet barrels delivered to the market were closer to 9 mb/d. HFIR notes the Saudis look like eager sellers and tanker rates have dropped, creating an overhang 'for now'.
items.angle: The 1.5 mb/d gap is going into storage or floating — it's the swing barrel for any de-escalation or escalation outcome.
items.tweetA: 10.5 mb/d produced, ~9 mb/d supplied. The missing 1.5 is the whole oil story right now: either it's a cushion if Hormuz-adjacent flows break, or it's the overhang that crushes price if the Iran deal sticks. Which one are you long? $XLE
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating Iran headlines. Nobody's debating where 1.5 mb/d of Saudi barrels went. That's a larger number than most OPEC+ 'cuts' people argue about for a week.

items.title: Lone Pine: +44% in H1, now -7% YTD
items.idea: Lone Pine rode AI to +44% in the first half of 2026, gave back all of it, and was down 7% YTD at end-October. Walleye is shutting its internal equity L/S teams, following exits from discretionary macro, commodities and credit in 2024/25.
items.angle: A 51-point swing in four months for a top-tier L/S book is the clearest fingerprint of the AI crowded-long unwind.
items.tweetA: +44% to -7% in four months. Lone Pine didn't get the thesis wrong — it got the exit wrong. That's the entire AI crowding story in one tear sheet. $NVDA $SMH
items.tweetB: Walleye closing equity L/S after already closing macro, commodities and credit. Pod shops are cutting verticals to one: factor-neutral dispersion. Who's left to short the crowded longs?

items.title: Concentration is marvelous until it isn't — Deutsche Boerse 2008 redux
items.idea: Rupak recalls when Lone Pine, TCI, Egerton and Viking together owned ~50% of Deutsche Boerse; in the GFC it underperformed massively as margin calls and redemptions forced selling. Egerton's Armitage: allocators love concentration because they run many funds, but 'when it goes wrong, boy, it's a disaster.'
items.angle: Allocator incentive (diversify across concentrated managers) is a hidden source of correlated forced selling.
items.tweetA: Allocators diversify across funds; funds concentrate within them. Result: the same 15 names owned by every 'diversified' book. The first redemption is everyone's margin call.
items.tweetB: In 2008 four hedge funds owned half of Deutsche Boerse. Today swap in the top-10 AI longs. The forced-seller dynamic is the same — only the ticker changed.

items.title: AI revenue is $345bn run-rate, 4.2x in a year — Anthropic's 'stall' is the market rate
items.idea: AI revenue hit $188bn over the twelve months to October and now runs at $345bn annualised, 4.2x a year ago (~43% per quarter). Anthropic's quarterly growth slowed from 147% to 45% — which Azeem argues is just the pace of the whole market; the 147% was the outlier. YoY it's still ~1,000%.
items.angle: Reframes the 'Anthropic decelerates' narrative: it converged to the industry curve. Important for IPO pricing debates.
items.tweetA: Anthropic growth 'slowed' from 147% to 45% a quarter. The whole AI economy is compounding ~43% a quarter. Slowing to the market rate isn't a stall — it's the base rate for a $345bn industry.
items.tweetB: $345bn run-rate AI revenue vs ~$1.4T of 2027 tech capex. Revenue is growing 4x a year; capex is being debated for a 5-7% haircut. Which of those two numbers does the sell-off actually reflect?

items.title: 'Flight to quality, not collapse': Democrats make data centers dearer, hyperscalers win, neoclouds are the weak link
items.idea: Azeem's view after the midterms and the Huang scandal: spending keeps rising; Democratic policy raises data-center costs which favours hyperscalers; Nvidia gets its wings clipped, and the open-weight camp with it; an Anthropic IPO at a sensible price would steady the sector; neoclouds are the weak link. Non-tech enterprises plan to spend more on AI next year than this year.
items.angle: A clean winners/losers map: hyperscalers > Nvidia > neoclouds / open-weight. Tradable pair thinking.
items.tweetA: If higher data-center costs are a barrier to entry, the biggest balance sheets win. That's a regulation-driven moat for $MSFT $GOOGL $AMZN and a margin squeeze for levered neoclouds like $CRWV.
items.tweetB: The market sold all of AI as one trade. Azeem's right that it's three: hyperscalers (moat), Nvidia (key-person + policy), neoclouds (leverage). Only one of those has a funding problem.

items.title: Sequoia unwinds 20 years of expansion; Thinking Machines nears $5B at $40B
items.idea: Jason's read: Sequoia shut Scouts and Arc because no one wants to run them after Roelof Botha's exit, not as punishment. Also listed: Thinking Machines nearing a $5B round at $40B, Nous Research's Arete-27B, Tesla winding down Cybertruck for Cybercab, and 'dueling proofs' from OpenAI and Anthropic astounding mathematicians.
items.angle: Venture is bifurcating: platform franchises retrenching while frontier-lab rounds scale. Key-person dependence shows up everywhere this week.
items.tweetA: Sequoia is shutting Scouts and Arc while Thinking Machines raises $5B at $40B. Venture's barbell: retreat from breadth, pile into a handful of lab-scale bets.
items.tweetB: Programs die when the founder leaves, not when they fail. Botha at Sequoia, Huang at Nvidia — it's the same lesson: what does your org look like with the key person removed?

items.title: 'Assume you're a target': honeypots and the Huang/Megaspeed story
items.idea: TWiST takeaway: influential people should assume they're targets, and bad actors may go through people one or two steps removed — an investor or an IT admin with keys. Context is Nvidia's board probe into Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and chip buyer Megaspeed.
items.angle: Supply-chain and export-control exposure now includes human-intelligence risk at the CEO level — a new category for compliance and governance premia.
items.tweetA: The threat model for AI isn't just export controls on chips. It's the people who control the allocation of chips. Megaspeed is the story to watch, not the affair.
items.tweetB: Kompromat on a CEO who decides who gets GPUs is a national-security issue. Expect congressional scrutiny of every allocation decision Nvidia made in China-adjacent channels. $NVDA

items.title: Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures: audit how labs split compute between R&D, safety, and inference
items.idea: AI Futures proposes VCAD: labs regularly report, with third-party verification, how compute is split across AI R&D, safety R&D, and external inference. Their claim: VCAD is needed to verify nearly any non-extreme pacing rule, and slowing software progress (not just training runs) avoids a 'software overhang' that could burst or be stolen by China.
items.angle: If Democrats pursue AI oversight, a compute-accounting standard is the most implementable first rule — and it would reveal inference-vs-R&D mix, a number investors lack today.
items.tweetA: If VCAD becomes law, we finally get audited numbers for how much compute is R&D vs. revenue-generating inference. That's the AI capex ROI disclosure the sell-side has been guessing at.
items.tweetB: Delay training runs without slowing software and you build a 'software overhang' — progress waiting to burst out. Regulating chips alone is regulating the wrong input.

items.title: 54,498 SPY Nov-13 $715 puts added
items.idea: TMAD flags a build of 54,498 contracts in SPY Nov 13 $715 puts — significant downside positioning below market — ahead of October CPI (consensus +0.3% m/m headline, +0.2% core).
items.angle: A single-strike put build into CPI = hedging or a directional bet on a hot print; watch dealer gamma around the strike.
items.tweetA: 54k SPY $715 puts for Nov 13 into CPI. Either someone is paying for protection after a $3T drawdown, or someone knows CPI risk is skewed. Strike matters more than size.
items.tweetB: When a market just lost $3T in two sessions, buying downside after the move is a hedger's tell — not a speculator's. The squeeze risk is to the downside hedgers.

items.title: October CPI: no y/y headline or core because Oct-2025 data is missing
items.idea: Because of the government shutdown, October 2025 price data are missing, so the y/y rates for October headline and core CPI aren't expected to be published. Only m/m (+0.3% / +0.2% consensus) are available.
items.angle: Base effects are unobservable — the market will trade m/m prints, and the Fed gets a data blackout on trend inflation.
items.tweetA: No y/y CPI this month. The inflation print the Fed cares most about literally doesn't exist, courtesy of last year's shutdown. Everyone trades the m/m and pretends it's not a problem.
items.tweetB: Shutdown data holes don't just delay prints — they delete a base year. Expect volatility in the next two CPI releases as seasonal/base math gets improvised.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: Goldman PB: stock pickers at five-year-low exposure, buybacks returning
items.idea: Goldman prime/trading desk: fundamental stock pickers have cut exposure to five-year lows, systematic strategies are set to sell more futures, and corporate buybacks are returning in size. But capitulation is incomplete: the largest tech positions remain crowded, broader ownership still substantial, and GS sentiment indicators aren't an unequivocal buy.
items.angle: A race between corporate bid and CTA/systematic supply decides the next leg.
items.tweetA: Fundamental managers at 5-year-low exposure, CTAs still selling, and corporate buybacks the only large bid. The recovery is a pure flows contest — not a thesis one.
items.tweetB: Low exposure, crowded top positions. That's the dangerous mix: the book looks light but the names that matter are the most owned. Capitulation isn't done until the crowded names break.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes
items.title: 'Stop bingo': ~$3T erased in two sessions on record volume
items.idea: Goldman's Bobby Molavi calls it 'stop bingo': falling P&L, broken relative-value trades and forced deleveraging across supposedly diversified books. Nearly $3T of US equity value vanished over two sessions while record volumes masked fragile liquidity. Molavi doubts it is a durable bottom; earnings are still decent, and AI rotation created valuation distortions in 'safe' areas.
items.angle: Volume ≠ liquidity. Record turnover on a forced-selling day means the opposite of depth.
items.tweetA: $3T gone in two days on record volume. Volume is not liquidity — it's the sound of everyone trying to leave through the same door. 'Stop bingo' is the best phrase of the quarter.
items.tweetB: Rotation out of AI created valuation extremes in defensive sectors. Staples at 23.6x forward vs Nvidia at ~10x isn't a rotation, it's a mispricing created by forced flows.

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: Nvidia at ~10x forward P/E — lowest since 2013; down $1.5T in a month
items.idea: Authers: Huang's scandal erased all Nvidia's gains since July of last year; market cap is down more than $1.5T in one month; blended forward P/E just above 10, lowest since 2013, vs S&P 500 at 17.7 and staples at 23.6. Nvidia failed to join the Nasdaq 100's 3.4% rally Monday — its worst relative day since DeepSeek. His point: no individual should be this important to a firm this size.
items.angle: Market is pricing key-person risk + policy risk; a sub-11x multiple on the dominant AI supplier is a contrarian setup if you believe the demand data.
items.tweetA: Nvidia trades at half the multiple of toasters and diapers (staples 23.6x vs NVDA ~10x). Either AI demand is about to break, or key-person fear is the cheapest option on the board. $NVDA
items.tweetB: $1.5T erased in a month and Nvidia still has no succession plan on the table. That's the real governance finding — the market is telling you the moat is a person, not the platform.

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: NY Fed: expected inflation 3.9% vs expected wage growth 2.6% — widest gap since 2013
items.idea: NY Fed consumer survey: 12-month inflation expectations 3.9% (too high for the Fed), but expected wage growth only 2.6%. Outside the post-pandemic bulge, that's the largest gap since 2013. Authers links this to the 'affordability crisis' and the election result: people have given up hoping pay keeps up.
items.angle: Real-income expectations, not CPI level, drive political outcomes — and consumption.
items.tweetA: Expected inflation 3.9%, expected raises 2.6%. A 1.3pt expected real pay cut is the midterm result in one chart. Consumer discretionary pricing power is the next casualty. $XLY
items.tweetB: The Fed targets inflation expectations; voters vote on wage expectations. They just diverged to the widest gap since 2013. Guess which one moves first?

charts.desc: NY Fed expected inflation vs expected wage growth gap

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: Milei's reelection odds slipped below 50% as US swap-line support looks fragile
items.idea: Last year's $20B Bessent-backed package helped Milei win midterms; a Democratic Congress can likely thwart repeat aid. Prediction markets now give his 2027 reelection slightly under 50% after being above for most of the year. Inflation is 34% (below 2019's level and below what he inherited); Merval in USD is flat over three years.
items.angle: Argentina is a clean read-through on how US political change reprices EM sovereigns that leaned on Washington.
items.tweetA: Argentina bonds are the first asset to price a Democratic Congress. The 2025 rescue was conditional on Milei winning; the 2027 rescue needs a Congress that doesn't exist.
items.tweetB: Flat Merval in dollars over 3 years after the most aggressive austerity in modern EM history. 'Boring Argentina' might be the most underrated outcome in the asset class.

charts.desc: Argentine bond yields, peso devaluation, Merval in USD, prediction market odds

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return (Richard Abbey)
items.title: EM vs US AI imports: 2001-02 saw a 55% collapse in US IT imports
items.idea: Oxford Economics' Sergi Lanau: EM domestic value-added embedded in US AI-related imports now dwarfs the dot-com boom, even GDP-adjusted. After 2000 US IT imports fell 55%. HSBC's Pinder argues midterm reaction is overdone since regulation slows capex rather than derails it. EM ex-China is +22% YTD but well below June highs; Taiwan restricted short selling, coinciding with Monday's rally.
items.angle: Taiwan/Korea are the transmission mechanism: an AI capex pause hits EM exports, not just US equities.
items.tweetA: US IT imports fell 55% after the dot-com bust. The AI import boom is bigger. Taiwan restricting short-selling on a rally day tells you how fragile the foundation is. $EWT $TSM
items.tweetB: EM got sold as 'the cheap AI trade'. EM ex-China is up 22% YTD on TSMC, Samsung and Hynix — it's a levered long of US capex budgets with a currency attached.

charts.desc: AI-related imports vs dot-com boom (domestic value added)

items.source: John Authers / Bloomberg Points of Return
items.title: The G in ESG makes a comeback: key-person risk, Tesla-SpaceX, and founder-control IPOs
items.idea: Authers: Huang's affair shows governance risk is not 'woke'. Massive IPOs are coming where founders want to keep control; a Tesla-SpaceX merger would require enormous trust in Musk. Ramaswamy's defeat in Ohio suggests the anti-woke backlash overshot as well.
items.angle: Governance discount could re-enter pricing for founder-controlled mega-IPOs (SpaceX, Anthropic?).
items.tweetA: Governance was dismissed as culture war until a CEO scandal took $1.5T off a stock in a month. Expect a governance discount in the mega-IPO pipeline. $TSLA
items.tweetB: Founder-control dual-class IPOs + key-person risk = the Nvidia repricing template. Who in the pipeline has a succession plan?

items.title: Cloud AI rug pull: 96% quota cut, $12k of tokens per $200 plan down to $2k
items.idea: Guest post: Grok Bot quota collapsed from 168 hours of continuous weekly use to 8 (−96%) after a switch to pricier Opus-5.5; Codex $200/mo plan value fell from ~$12k of API-equivalent tokens to ~$2k. Author claims labs cut quotas and raise prices every 6-10 weeks, and silently degrade models post-launch via quantisation.
items.angle: Evidence that subsidised consumption plans are ending; token pricing power shifting to labs - a margin tailwind for labs, a cost headwind for AI-native users.
items.tweetA: Effective tokens per $200 plan fell ~6x this year. That is a 6x price increase without a price increase. Inflation is hiding in the quota.
items.tweetB: Every 'AI is cheaper every quarter' chart ignores that plans get nerfed every 6-10 weeks. Unit cost down, effective price up — someone is capturing that spread. $AMZN $GOOGL

items.title: Local-AI hardware squeeze: DGX Spark $4k→$10k, M5 Ultra 512GB lead time 3 weeks→5 months
items.idea: Per the author: DGX Sparks went from $4k to ~$10k, used M3 Ultras doubled, M5 Ultra 512GB pre-orders opened Oct 28 and shipping slipped from 3 weeks to ~5 months; Micron cancelled another factory expansion. Break-even on $20k hardware vs $300/mo plans is 5.5 years, but 2 months at $10k/mo. Amazon warned compute stays tight into 2028.
items.angle: Cloud pricing pressure is spilling into consumer/prosumer memory demand — another leg for DRAM/HBM scarcity.
items.tweetA: Prosumer AI hardware is going the way of GPUs in 2021: DGX Spark 2.5x, Mac Studio lead times to 5 months. RAM is the bottleneck and Micron just cancelled capacity. $MU $AAPL
items.tweetB: Cloud plan prices up, hardware prices up, lead times up. The demand curve for tokens is so inelastic that people are buying $20k boxes to hedge it. That's not a bubble signal, it's a scarcity signal.

items.title: 100 PRs a year (2022) → 25,000 a year: engineering output at $140 per PR
items.idea: Author's trajectory: ~100 PRs/yr as a 2022 staff engineer, 100/month by end-2025, 100/week at a 2026 startup, now ~100 merged per day with agent teams — annualising to 25,000. At $140 of API cost per PR that's $3.5M of non-subsidised token spend, versus $3.6k/yr on plans. Claims a year's work for 6-10 senior engineers was done solo in two months.
items.angle: Quantifies agentic productivity and the real economic cost if subsidies end: labor substitution at $140/PR is still far cheaper than a $300k engineer.
items.tweetA: 25,000 PRs a year at $140 = $3.5M. Per PR, that's about 40 minutes of a senior engineer. Even at unsubsidised prices, the labor substitution math still works.
items.tweetB: Output per engineer went 250x in four years while salaries are flat. Where does the surplus go — to labs via pricing, or to the firms that deploy?

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: Google ships four TPU systems in a year; TPU sales seen $12B → $135B by 2028
items.idea: Google added the TPU 8tx (confidential compute with AMD EPYC, half the 8t latency) and TPU 8i Max (two 8i dies per package, double SRAM and HBM bandwidth) to the 8t (2.7x training) and 8i (80% better inference price-performance). Bloomberg Intelligence sees TPU sales topping $135B by 2028 from ~$12B this year; TPUs ~30% cheaper than Nvidia GPUs. Nearly 100 customers incl. Apple, Meta, Oracle; Anthropic has an option for up to $150B of TPUs 2028-31.
items.angle: A year ago Nvidia's moat was 'no alternative at scale'. $12B → $135B in 3 years is an 11x ramp.
items.tweetA: TPU sales: $12B this year, $135B by 2028 (BI). That's an 11x ramp from the one competitor with its own frontier model, 30% cheaper silicon, and nearly 100 customers. $GOOGL $NVDA
items.tweetB: Google shipped four TPU variants in a year; it used to be one every two years. Cadence is the moat — and it happens the week Nvidia's CEO is under board investigation.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: TPU bear case: every chip pre-sold, margins below Nvidia, post-midterm backlash cuts 2027 capex 5-7%
items.idea: Parekh lists Google's problems: lower TPU margins than Nvidia (BI), all TPUs already contracted, diversification beyond Broadcom to Marvell and reportedly MediaTek, new rival Tenspresso (ex-TPU engineers, 1+ year away), OpenAI/Anthropic making their own chips, and a data-center backlash that could shave the ~$1.4T expected 2027 tech spend by 5-7%.
items.angle: $70-100B swing in 2027 spend is the quantification of the policy risk everyone is hand-waving.
items.tweetA: 5-7% off $1.4T of 2027 capex is $70-100B. That's roughly Nvidia's entire quarterly revenue as the cost of one election. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: Google sells everything it makes, at lower margins than Nvidia, from a supply chain still constrained by memory. The bull case is a capacity story, not a demand story.

items.source: Michael Parekh / AI: Reset to Zero
items.title: Nvidia -6.6% intraday while Broadcom and AMD rose 6%+ and Alphabet +4.1%
items.idea: On the Huang probe news Nvidia fell as much as 6.6% while Broadcom and AMD, both Nvidia rivals, rose more than 6%, and Alphabet rose as much as 4.1%. Parekh warns not to over-read one day: Nvidia still has demand above supply. Customers planning 2027+ AI-chip purchases now have more reasons to diversify.
items.angle: Same-day rotation inside AI: Nvidia → ASIC/merchant alternatives is a trade, not a thesis-break.
items.tweetA: Nvidia -6.6%, $AVGO and $AMD +6%, $GOOGL +4%. The market just ran an unplanned stress test of the 'alternatives' thesis. It passed.
items.tweetB: Pair trade writes itself: long the diversification beneficiaries, short key-person risk. Problem is it also shows how little of the move is fundamental.
